case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the Second Circuit’s “right to control” theory—treating deprivation of accurate, decision-relevant economic information as a deprivation of property—states a valid basis for wire-fraud liability.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 18 U.S.C. § 1343 (federal wire fraud statute) (and, by implication, the scope of “money or property” within the federal fraud statutes).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Ciminelli argues the “right to control” theory is an impermissible expansion of federal fraud law because it converts an intangible interest in information (or in making informed economic decisions) into “property,” even when the alleged scheme does not aim to obtain traditional property or money. In petitioner’s view, the federal fraud statutes protect only traditional property rights, not an all-purpose right to receive complete and accurate information; allowing liability based on withheld or misleading information untethered to a property transfer effectively federalizes broad swaths of sharp dealing and regulatory/non-disclosure disputes beyond the statute’s text and historical limits.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The United States argues that schemes depriving a victim of economically valuable information necessary to make discretionary economic decisions can constitute property fraud because the victim’s ability to control its assets through informed decisionmaking has economic value; thus, interference with that interest can satisfy the “money or property” element of wire fraud. The government also generally maintains that the jury instructions and theory used in the prosecution fit within valid understandings of wire fraud and do not improperly create an “ethereal,” free-floating interest divorced from economic harm.
key_precedents: United States v. Binday, 804 F.3d 558 (2d Cir. 2015)

John Roberts.reasoning: The best respondent move remains the Carpenter analogy—that valuable information can be “property”—but, as Justice Kavanaugh stresses, Carpenter involved appropriation of a classic proprietary asset (confidential business information) as the object of the scheme, not an abstract entitlement to better decisionmaking. Our line from McNally through Cleveland and Kelly, echoed by Justice Barrett, cautions against converting regulatory or decisional interests into “property” without a clear congressional statement, and the Second Circuit’s “right to control” theory lacks a principled limiting line. Justice Kagan’s narrow, administrable approach preserves legitimate prosecutions where the scheme aims to obtain money or traditional property (including true proprietary information) while rejecting “right to control” as a standalone theory. Nothing raised in conference undermines that minimal holding, and it best serves fair notice and institutional legitimacy in a criminal statute.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The strongest conceivable argument for Respondent is that § 1343 should cover schemes that deprive victims of economically valuable information because information can be “property,” as in Carpenter. But, as Justice Kavanaugh notes, Carpenter involved a classic proprietary interest—confidential business information that the defendant sought to appropriate—whereas the Second Circuit’s “right to control” theory treats an abstract interest in better-informed decisionmaking as property without any traditional, transferable property object. Justice Gorsuch’s separation-of-powers and lenity concerns reinforce the textual point: expanding “money or property” to include amorphous decisionmaking interests lacks a limiting principle and effectively federalizes ordinary deceit absent a clear congressional statement. Under an original public meaning approach, “property” in § 1343 cannot be stretched to cover a free-floating right to accurate information untethered to obtaining traditional property.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The respondent’s best point remains that deception causing economically worse choices effectively deprives a victim of a property interest, but that theory collapses § 1343’s “money or property” requirement into an amorphous right to accurate information, the same untethered expansion we rejected in McNally and Cleveland. Justice Kavanaugh’s distinction to Carpenter is decisive for me: Carpenter involved appropriation of a recognized proprietary asset (confidential business information), whereas “right to control” treats the victim’s impaired decisionmaking as the property itself without any traditional property being targeted for acquisition. Chief Justice Roberts’s practical-consequences concern reinforces the textual point—accepting “right to control” would federalize vast swaths of ordinary commercial sharp dealing and disclosure disputes absent a clear congressional statement. Nothing in colleagues’ discussion undermines the core statutory object requirement that the scheme aim to obtain traditional money or property, not merely to influence choices.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The best respondent argument—that economically valuable information is “property” and that depriving it distorts how a victim deploys assets—still fails because it effectively converts § 1343 into a general federal ban on sharp dealing and nondisclosure, with no workable limiting principle. Justice Kagan’s administrability concern crystallizes the problem: if the “property” is simply the victim’s interest in better-informed decisionmaking, nearly every commercial lie becomes wire fraud, which our fair-notice cases (McNally, Cleveland, Kelly) reject absent a clear congressional statement. Justice Kavanaugh and the Chief Justice persuasively distinguish Carpenter, where the scheme targeted and appropriated a recognized proprietary asset (confidential business information) as the object, not an abstract “right to control” choices. Under a pragmatic lens attentive to real-world impacts, an amorphous theory that invites arbitrary, expansive criminal enforcement would predictably fall hardest on vulnerable defendants and erode consistent access to justice, so I would reject “right to control” while preserving prosecutions aimed at obtaining traditional money or property.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The respondent’s best shot is the Carpenter-based claim that economically valuable information is “property,” so depriving a party of decision-relevant facts should qualify. But as Justice Kavanaugh (and the Chief) emphasize, Carpenter involved appropriation of a recognized proprietary asset—confidential business information—as the object of the scheme, whereas the Second Circuit’s “right to control” theory elevates an abstract interest in better decisionmaking into property even when the victim gets the bargained-for goods and no transferable asset is targeted. Justice Barrett’s reliance on Kelly and Cleveland reinforces that our line is about object: deception that influences choices is not enough unless obtaining money or traditional property is what the scheme aims to get. Textually and administrably, I still think the workable middle ground is to reject “right to control” as standalone property while leaving intact prosecutions where the object is money or traditional property (including true proprietary information).

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The strongest respondent argument would be that deception that induces a victim to enter a transaction necessarily targets the victim’s money, so “right to control” is just a way of describing economic harm; but § 1343 requires the object of the scheme to be obtaining money or property, not merely impairing decisionmaking through withheld information. Justice Kavanaugh’s Carpenter distinction is important: confidential business information can be “property” because it is a recognized proprietary asset the defendant seeks to appropriate, whereas the Second Circuit’s “right to control” reframes an abstract interest in better-informed choices as property, untethered to a traditional property right. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett stress via Cleveland and Kelly, we have insisted on a clear limiting principle and a clear congressional statement before expanding federal fraud into generalized sharp dealing. On a textualist and originalist reading, “money or property” does not naturally include an amorphous right to accurate information, and the rule of lenity counsels against the respondent’s broader construction.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The strongest counterargument for Respondent would be that deceptive deprivation of economically valuable information can itself be “property” under Carpenter, but that case involved classic proprietary information the defendant sought to appropriate, not a free-floating interest in better decisionmaking. Chief Justice Roberts’s point about institutional legitimacy and the need for a clear limiting principle is persuasive: the Second Circuit’s “right to control” theory risks recreating the broad intangible-rights approach rejected in McNally and invites the federalization concerns emphasized in Cleveland. Justice Barrett’s citation to Kelly reinforces the same doctrinal line—deception that affects allocation or decisionmaking authority is not wire fraud unless the object is to obtain money or traditional property. Under text, precedent, and practical administrability, “right to control” cannot stand as an independent property theory under § 1343.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest point would be that “property” in § 1343 can include intangibles, and Carpenter confirms that proposition. But as Justice Kavanaugh explains, Carpenter involved a classic proprietary interest—confidential business information that the defendant sought to appropriate—whereas the Second Circuit’s “right to control” theory treats the victim’s desire for accurate information to make better choices as the property itself, untethered to obtaining a traditional, transferable property interest. That move runs headlong into McNally, Cleveland, and Kelly, which insist that the object of the scheme must be to obtain money or property, not merely to influence decisionmaking or governance. Even accepting that deception can induce a victim to part with money, the “right to control” theory cannot serve as an independent property basis without an administrable limiting principle and a clear congressional statement.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The strongest respondent contention—invoking Carpenter to say economically valuable information is “property”—still fails because, as Justice Kavanaugh emphasizes, Carpenter involved appropriation of a recognized proprietary asset, not an abstract entitlement to better decisionmaking. Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan’s administrability concerns matter to me as a progressive pragmatist: the Second Circuit’s “right to control” theory supplies no workable limiting principle and risks arbitrary, discriminatory enforcement in routine commercial disputes—especially troubling in criminal prosecutions. Our precedents (McNally, Cleveland, Kelly) draw a consistent line requiring that the scheme’s object be obtaining money or traditional property, not merely causing a victim to make a less-informed choice. That framework preserves fair notice and keeps § 1343 from becoming a general federal remedy for sharp dealing absent a clear congressional directive.

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 1343 requires a scheme to obtain "money or property," and our precedents caution against reading that phrase to encompass abstract, decisionmaking or regulatory interests untethered to traditional property attributes. In Cleveland v. United States, 531 U.S. 12 (2000), we rejected treating a state’s licensing interest as “property” for fraud purposes, emphasizing the need for a clear congressional statement before expanding federal criminal jurisdiction into areas traditionally regulated by the States. The Second Circuit’s “right to control” theory effectively converts a generalized interest in receiving accurate information into “property,” risking the same sweeping expansion and prosecutorial discretion concerns that motivated McNally and our narrowing approach in Skilling. A narrow holding invalidating “right to control” as an independent property theory best accords with the statutory text, precedent, and institutional legitimacy.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The text of 18 U.S.C. § 1343 reaches only schemes to obtain “money or property,” and the Second Circuit’s “right to control” theory improperly recasts an amorphous interest in accurate, decision-relevant information as “property” untethered to any traditional property right. This Court has held the federal fraud statutes are “carefully circumscribed” to protect property rights and rejected intangible-rights theories, see McNally v. United States, 483 U.S. 350 (1987), and has continued to insist that the object of the scheme must be to obtain property, not merely to influence decisionmaking. Treating diminished “economic decisionmaking” as property expands federal criminal jurisdiction beyond the statute’s original public meaning, raises fair-notice concerns, and invites federalization of state-law deceit and regulatory disputes. Accordingly, the “right to control” theory does not state a valid basis for wire-fraud liability under § 1343.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 1343 requires a scheme to obtain “money or property,” and the Second Circuit’s “right to control” theory effectively converts an amorphous interest in accurate, decision-relevant information into “property,” untethered to the acquisition of traditional property interests. This Court has repeatedly rejected such expansions of the federal fraud statutes beyond traditional property rights, emphasizing that they should not be read to federalize broad swaths of sharp dealing or regulatory/non-disclosure disputes. In Cleveland v. United States, the Court refused to treat an intangible governmental/regulatory interest as “property” for fraud purposes, and McNally likewise confined the statutes to the protection of property rights absent clear congressional authorization. Congress’s targeted response to McNally in 18 U.S.C. § 1346 (honest-services fraud) underscores that courts should not create additional intangible-rights theories—like “right to control”—under § 1343.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 1343 requires a scheme to obtain "money or property," and this Court has repeatedly refused to expand that phrase to cover free-floating, intangible interests in sound government or decisionmaking. Cleveland v. United States held that the fraud statutes do not treat regulatory or decisionmaking interests as property, and McNally similarly rejected treating intangible rights as "property" under the fraud laws; the Second Circuit’s “right to control” theory risks recreating that prohibited expansion by turning deprivation of accurate information into property loss even without a targeted transfer of traditional property. Allowing liability on this theory also threatens fair notice and invites arbitrary enforcement—concerns this Court underscored when it narrowed § 1346 in Skilling to avoid vagueness and overcriminalization. Whatever the misconduct here, stretching § 1343 to cover it would federalize broad swaths of sharp dealing better handled by more tailored statutes or state law, with serious practical consequences for even ordinary commercial disputes.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 1343 reaches only schemes whose object is to obtain “money or property,” and this Court has repeatedly rejected theories that convert decisionmaking or regulatory interests into property for federal fraud purposes. As in McNally and Cleveland, the Second Circuit’s “right to control” theory risks untethering “property” from traditional, transferable economic interests by treating the withholding of decision-relevant information itself as the deprivation, even where the victim receives the benefit of the bargain and no property is targeted as the object of the scheme. That approach is textually and administratively unworkable because it would federalize wide swaths of sharp dealing and disclosure disputes without a clear limiting principle, contrary to the coherent, bounded reading of “money or property” in the fraud statutes. A workable middle ground remains available: the government may prosecute where the scheme aims to obtain the victim’s money or traditional property by deception, but not where the only asserted “property” is the victim’s abstract right to make better-informed choices.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 1343 criminalizes schemes to obtain “money or property,” and its plain text does not naturally encompass an abstract “right to control” assets through receipt of accurate, decision-relevant information untethered to the acquisition of traditional property. This Court has repeatedly resisted expanding the fraud statutes to cover intangible or regulatory interests absent clear congressional direction, including in Cleveland v. United States (rejecting treating state licensing interests as “property”) and McNally (rejecting intangible-rights theories), with § 1346 supplying only a narrow, separate carveout. Allowing the Second Circuit’s theory would effectively federalize broad swaths of sharp dealing and nondisclosure and would invite the sort of indeterminacy Skilling warned against, all contrary to separation-of-powers principles and the rule of lenity in construing criminal statutes. Because the government’s theory would stretch “property” beyond its original and ordinary meaning, the conviction cannot rest on “right to control” as a standalone basis for wire-fraud liability.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Section 1343 requires a scheme to obtain “money or property,” and our precedents caution against expanding that element to cover generalized interests in accurate information or informed decisionmaking untethered to a traditional property interest. In Cleveland v. United States, 531 U.S. 12 (2000), and McNally v. United States, 483 U.S. 350 (1987), the Court rejected interpretations of the federal fraud statutes that would convert nontraditional or regulatory/intangible interests into “property,” in part to avoid a sweeping expansion of federal criminal jurisdiction. While Carpenter v. United States, 484 U.S. 19 (1987), recognizes that some intangible interests can be “property,” it involved a classic proprietary interest (confidential business information) that the defendant sought to appropriate, not an open-ended “right to control” theory premised on deprivation of decision-relevant information. The Second Circuit’s “right to control” theory is difficult to cabin and risks federalizing broad swaths of sharp dealing and disclosure disputes better left to state law and specific federal statutes, contrary to history, tradition, and practical workability.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Section 1343 reaches only schemes to obtain “money or property,” and this Court has repeatedly refused to treat intangible interests in sound governance or regulatory decisionmaking as “property” absent clear statutory direction. McNally v. United States, Cleveland v. United States, and Kelly v. United States each reject efforts to expand the fraud statutes beyond traditional property concepts, emphasizing that any further extension must come from Congress. The Second Circuit’s “right to control” theory effectively redefines “property” to include deprivation of accurate, decision-relevant information untethered to a traditional property transfer, which is inconsistent with the statute’s text and the Court’s methodological line drawing. Because the theory permits conviction without a scheme aimed at obtaining money or traditional property, it is not a valid basis for wire-fraud liability under § 1343.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Section 1343 requires a scheme to obtain “money or property,” and this Court has repeatedly declined to stretch “property” to cover diffuse, intangible interests untethered to traditional property rights. Under Cleveland v. United States, 531 U.S. 12 (2000), and Kelly v. United States, 140 S. Ct. 1565 (2020), the fraud statutes do not criminalize deception that merely affects decisionmaking authority or regulatory-style control absent an object of obtaining property; the Second Circuit’s “right to control” theory similarly treats accurate information as property and risks federalizing broad sharp-dealing and nondisclosure disputes. That expansion also threatens fair-notice and arbitrary-enforcement concerns identified in Skilling v. United States, 561 U.S. 358 (2010), by allowing prosecutors to repackage amorphous dishonesty as “property” fraud without a clear limiting principle. Given the statute’s text and these precedents, deprivation of decision-relevant information alone is not a valid basis for wire-fraud liability under § 1343.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the Second Circuit’s “right to control” theory—treating the deprivation of potentially valuable economic information affecting a victim’s decisionmaking as “property” loss—validly supports wire-fraud liability.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 18 U.S.C. § 1343 (federal wire fraud statute) (and, as background in related petitions, 18 U.S.C. § 1346 (honest-services fraud)).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Ciminelli argues that the federal fraud statutes criminalize only schemes to obtain traditional money or property, not schemes that merely deprive a victim of accurate information relevant to making an economic decision. The Second Circuit’s right-to-control doctrine improperly converts an “ethereal” interest in informed decisionmaking into a property right, vastly expanding federal fraud beyond its textual and historical limits and effectively creating an all-purpose federal business-ethics code. Under proper interpretation, misinformation in a bidding or contracting process is not wire fraud unless it is aimed at obtaining money/property in the traditional sense (or otherwise causes a concrete property loss), and jury instructions allowing conviction based on “deprivation of information” alone are invalid.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The United States defends the convictions by arguing that the scheme targeted the victim’s property interests as recognized in Second Circuit doctrine: the victim’s right to control its assets by making informed economic decisions. Under that view, depriving the victim of economically valuable information that is necessary to discretionary spending decisions is itself a cognizable property harm under § 1343, because it exposes the victim to economic risk and can lead it to allocate money differently than it otherwise would. Thus, the government contends the jury instructions reflecting the right-to-control concept stated a valid money-or-property fraud theory and fit within established circuit precedent.
key_precedents: United States v. Binday, 804 F.3d 558 (2d Cir. 2015)

John Roberts.reasoning: The strongest counterargument is that depriving a counterparty of economically valuable information is itself a property harm because it can predictably affect the price or terms of a deal; but that collapses § 1343’s “money or property” element into a general prohibition on sharp dealing, contrary to McNally’s limiting principle and our refusal in Cleveland and Kelly to treat decisionmaking control as property. Justice Kagan’s warning about converting any “economically relevant lie” into federal wire fraud underscores the administrability and legitimacy problem with the Second Circuit’s right-to-control theory. Carpenter does not change that conclusion because it involved recognized property—confidential business information—where the object was to appropriate the information itself, not merely to influence a victim’s discretion with incomplete or misleading facts. A narrow holding vacating the convictions is warranted because the jury could convict without finding an object to obtain traditional money or property, and Congress—not this Court—should decide whether to criminalize that broader category.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The strongest conceivable argument for respondent is that economically valuable information can be treated as “property,” invoking Carpenter, and that deception in bidding effectively obtains money by inducing a contract. But as Justice Gorsuch notes, § 1343’s original public meaning focused on traditional property interests and the obtaining of them; the Second Circuit’s “right to control” theory instead converts the victim’s interest in informed decisionmaking into the property itself, which McNally, Cleveland, and Kelly reject. Carpenter is consistent with that line because it involved a recognized property interest—confidential business information—rather than an abstract entitlement to accurate information in negotiations. I agree with Chief Justice Roberts that adopting right-to-control would erase the statute’s limiting principle and effectively create a federal business-ethics code without clear congressional authorization, contrary to text, history, and lenity.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The strongest likely respondent argument is that depriving a counterparty of economically valuable information is effectively a property harm because it predictably affects the price paid or the allocation of scarce resources; but § 1343 requires that the scheme’s object be to obtain “money or property,” not merely to induce a less-informed decision, and Cleveland and Kelly reject converting control over decisions into property. Justice Gorsuch’s point about lenity reinforces that any ambiguity about treating “information” as property must be resolved against expanding criminal liability beyond traditional property concepts, especially given Congress’s targeted use of § 1346 rather than a broader informational-fraud provision. Carpenter does not save the right-to-control theory because it involved recognized property (confidential business information) being taken, whereas here the Second Circuit’s doctrine treats the victim’s interest in accurate information as property in itself. Like Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, adopting the right-to-control theory would effectively federalize ordinary commercial misstatements without a clear statutory hook, an overbreadth this Court has repeatedly resisted.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The strongest respondent claim—that economically valuable information is “property” because it affects price and risk—still collapses § 1343’s money-or-property element into a sweeping ban on any economically relevant lie. Chief Justice Roberts’s reliance on McNally, Cleveland, and Kelly is decisive for me: those cases draw a firm boundary against treating decisionmaking autonomy or “control” as property, even when real economic consequences follow. Carpenter does not undermine that limit, as Justice Thomas and Justice Kagan explain, because it involved the taking of a recognized property interest (confidential business information) rather than mere deception that induces a bargain. Pragmatically, adopting right-to-control would predictably expand federal criminal exposure for ordinary commercial sharp dealing in ways that disproportionately harm less-resourced defendants and provide poor notice, so I remain with petitioner.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The best respondent point is the “bid-rigging lie naturally aims at money” idea—because the defendant wants a paid contract and deception can predictably worsen the victim’s economic position—but that still conflates the statute’s object requirement with downstream economic effects. As Chief Justice Roberts stresses, treating any economically relevant misinformation as “property” dissolves § 1343’s money-or-property boundary into a materiality test and effectively federalizes ordinary commercial sharp dealing, which McNally’s limiting principle and our refusals in Cleveland and Kelly to constitutionalize decisionmaking control as property counsel against. Justice Thomas’s distinction to Carpenter is important for my pragmatic textualist line: we can recognize certain intangible assets as property when the scheme targets the asset itself (confidential business information), without redefining “property” to include an abstract entitlement to accurate negotiating inputs. Because the jury here could convict on deprivation of “potentially valuable economic information” alone, the convictions cannot stand under the most administrable, text-coherent reading of § 1343.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The strongest pushback I anticipate from the respondent is that economically valuable information can be “property,” but Carpenter treated confidential business information as a recognized, tradable asset—not an abstract entitlement to make better decisions. As Justice Thomas emphasizes, McNally, Cleveland, and Kelly require that the object of the scheme be to obtain traditional money or property; the Second Circuit’s “right to control” theory instead criminalizes deception that merely affects a victim’s discretion. Chief Justice Roberts is also right that this approach lacks a limiting principle and risks converting ordinary sharp dealing into a federal felony absent clear congressional authorization. Where § 1343 is at least doubtful on this intangible theory, the rule of lenity reinforces adhering to the statute’s historically grounded money-or-property requirement.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The best counterargument for Respondent is that depriving a victim of economically valuable information in a commercial setting effectively exposes the victim to tangible economic harm and should count as “property,” but that collapses the statute’s money-or-property element into mere materiality and risks making § 1343 a general business-ethics code. Chief Justice Roberts is right that Cleveland and Kelly draw a firm line between schemes aimed at obtaining property and schemes aimed at influencing discretionary decisionmaking, and the Second Circuit’s “right to control” theory sits on the wrong side of that line. Justice Thomas’s comparison to Carpenter reinforces that we can recognize certain intangible property (confidential business information) without redefining “property” to include an abstract entitlement to accurate information. Given precedent, history, and administrability, I would adhere to a clear rule that § 1343 does not reach the standalone deprivation of decisionmaking information untethered to obtaining traditional property.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The strongest respondent-side contention would be that depriving a counterparty of economically valuable information is functionally equivalent to taking property because it can alter the price or terms of a deal. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, our precedents (McNally, Cleveland, Kelly) require the object of the scheme to be obtaining money or property in the victim’s hands, not an abstract interest in informed discretion, and the Second Circuit’s “right to control” theory collapses that limit by redefining decisionmaking autonomy as “property.” Justice Thomas’s distinction to Carpenter is persuasive: confidential business information may be property, but “potentially valuable economic information” that merely informs a choice is not a traditionally recognized property interest that § 1343 targets. On a textualist/originalist reading, and with lenity concerns noted by Justice Gorsuch in the background, the jury instruction allowing conviction without finding an aim to obtain traditional property cannot stand.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The respondent’s best point—that economically valuable information should count as “property” because its concealment predictably affects price—still runs into the limiting principle Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize: Cleveland and Kelly require that the object of the scheme be obtaining traditional money or property, not merely manipulating a counterparty’s discretion with distorted inputs. Carpenter does not bridge that gap because, as Justice Thomas explains, it involved appropriation of a recognized property interest (confidential business information) rather than treating any decision-relevant information as property. From a procedural-fairness and administrability perspective, the Second Circuit’s right-to-control theory risks turning material misstatements in ordinary commerce into federal felonies without clear notice or a workable boundary. Given the jury could convict without finding an object to obtain money or property as traditionally understood, the convictions cannot stand under § 1343’s text and our precedents.

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 1343 reaches only schemes to obtain “money or property,” and this Court has repeatedly refused to expand that element to cover intangible interests in decisionmaking control untethered to a traditional property interest. Cleveland v. United States held that an interest in controlling governmental decisionmaking is not “property” for purposes of the fraud statutes, and Kelly v. United States likewise rejected liability where the object was regulatory control rather than obtaining property. The Second Circuit’s “right to control” theory risks converting any material misrepresentation in commercial negotiations into federal wire fraud, undermining limiting principles and institutional legitimacy by effectively creating a broad federal business-ethics code absent congressional authorization (contrast 18 U.S.C. § 1346’s narrow restoration of honest-services fraud). A narrow ruling vacating the convictions is appropriate because deprivation of “potentially valuable economic information,” standing alone, is not the requisite property object under § 1343.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The text of 18 U.S.C. § 1343 reaches schemes to obtain “money or property,” and that phrase must be given its ordinary, traditional meaning rather than expanded to cover an abstract “right to control” decisionmaking. As McNally v. United States held, the fraud statutes “protect[] property rights only” and do not criminalize deprivations of intangible interests untethered to traditional property; this Court has repeatedly rejected similar efforts to convert regulatory or informational interests into “property.” See McNally, 483 U.S. at 356, 358–59; Cleveland v. United States, 531 U.S. 12, 18–20; Kelly v. United States, 140 S. Ct. 1565, 1571–72. Unlike Carpenter, where confidential business information was a recognized property interest, the Second Circuit’s right-to-control theory treats potentially valuable information affecting discretion as property itself and thereby creates an open-ended federal business-ethics code without clear congressional authorization.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 1343 targets schemes “for obtaining money or property,” and the Second Circuit’s “right to control” theory redefines “property” to include an intangible interest in receiving accurate economic information—an expansion not supported by the statute’s text. This Court has repeatedly rejected attempts to stretch the fraud statutes beyond traditional property interests, warning against turning them into a broad federal business-ethics code. In Cleveland v. United States, the Court declined to treat nontraditional, regulatory or intangible interests as “property” for fraud purposes, and Congress’s targeted enactment of § 1346 to cover only “honest services” confirms it did not silently criminalize other informational interests. Practical consequences also counsel against the doctrine because it would federalize commonplace misrepresentations in commercial dealings without a clear showing that the object of the scheme was to obtain traditional money or property.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 1343 reaches schemes to obtain “money or property,” and this Court has repeatedly rejected efforts to stretch that term to cover abstract decisionmaking or regulatory interests untethered to a traditional property object. Cleveland v. United States and Kelly v. United States teach that a victim’s interest in controlling how it exercises discretion—whether regulatory or managerial—does not become “property” simply because deception influenced the decision. The Second Circuit’s “right to control” theory risks criminalizing broad swaths of sharp dealing without requiring the government to prove the object of the scheme was to obtain identifiable money or property, raising the same overbreadth and notice concerns this Court addressed by narrowing intangible-interest fraud in Skilling (and leaving other intangibles to Congress, as in Cleveland). Fairness and administrability favor a clear rule: misrepresentations in a bidding process are wire fraud only when aimed at obtaining traditional property (or causing a concrete property loss), not merely depriving a victim of “potentially valuable” information.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 1343 targets schemes to obtain “money or property,” and this Court has repeatedly declined to stretch “property” to cover intangible interests in decisionmaking or regulatory control. Cleveland v. United States and Kelly v. United States reject treating control over choices or processes as property where the object is not a traditional property interest; the Second Circuit’s “right to control” theory similarly risks converting any economically relevant lie into federal wire fraud. Skilling v. United States underscores the need to cabin federal fraud doctrines to avoid creating an all-purpose code of business ethics untethered from statutory text, and Congress’s targeted response in § 1346 counsels against expanding § 1343 by judicial invention. The workable, coherent line is that deception in bidding can be prosecuted under § 1343 only when aimed at obtaining traditional money/property or causing a concrete property loss, not merely depriving a party of information affecting its discretion.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 1343 reaches only schemes to obtain “money or property,” and at the time of enactment that language referred to traditional property interests, not an abstract entitlement to accurate information to guide decisionmaking. This Court has repeatedly refused to expand the fraud statutes to cover intangible interests untethered to property, as in McNally and Cleveland, and Kelly likewise confirms that the statute targets the obtaining of property, not the manipulation of how a victim exercises discretion. The Second Circuit’s “right to control” theory effectively treats the deprivation of economically useful information as property itself, creating a roving federal business-ethics code that Congress has not enacted and raising the same vagueness and overbreadth concerns that drove Skilling’s narrowing of § 1346. At minimum, where § 1343 is ambiguous about such an intangible theory, the rule of lenity counsels against extending criminal liability beyond traditional money-or-property fraud.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Section 1343 reaches only schemes to obtain “money or property,” and this Court has repeatedly refused to extend the federal fraud statutes to intangible interests untethered to traditional property concepts. McNally v. United States held that the fraud statutes protect “property rights only,” not amorphous interests like the public’s “intangible right” to good government, and Cleveland v. United States similarly rejected efforts to treat regulatory or discretionary interests as “property” for fraud purposes. The Second Circuit’s “right to control” theory effectively criminalizes deprivation of accurate information in decisionmaking—an interest too “ethereal” to qualify as property under McNally—and risks turning § 1343 into a sweeping federal business-ethics code. Whatever the practical appeal of policing bid-process deception, judicial restraint and workability counsel adhering to the statute’s historically grounded money-or-property limitation unless Congress clearly expands it.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Section 1343, read according to its text and original public meaning, reaches schemes "for obtaining money or property"; it does not criminalize the mere deprivation of accurate information bearing on a victim’s decisionmaking. McNally v. United States limited the fraud statutes to traditional property interests, and Cleveland v. United States and Kelly v. United States reinforced that the object of the fraud must be property in the victim’s hands, not an abstract entitlement to sound governance or informed choices. The Second Circuit’s “right to control” doctrine effectively converts an ethereal interest in decisionmaking into "property," expanding federal fraud beyond the statute’s limits and blurring the line between deception and property-taking. Because the jury could convict based on withheld economically relevant information without finding an aim to obtain traditional money or property, the theory cannot validly support wire-fraud liability under § 1343.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Section 1343 targets schemes “for obtaining money or property,” and this Court has repeatedly rejected efforts to expand the fraud statutes beyond traditional property interests into more “ethereal” or regulatory interests. Under Cleveland v. United States, 531 U.S. 12 (2000), and McNally v. United States, 483 U.S. 350 (1987), depriving a victim of information that might influence discretionary decisionmaking—without aiming to obtain a traditional property interest—cannot itself be treated as a standalone “property” loss. While Carpenter v. United States, 484 U.S. 19 (1987), recognizes certain intangible property (e.g., confidential business information), the Second Circuit’s right-to-control theory risks collapsing ordinary misrepresentations into federal wire fraud in a way that undermines fair notice and practical limits on prosecutorial discretion. Procedural fairness and workable boundaries counsel reversing convictions that rested on jury instructions permitting conviction based on deprivation of economically valuable information alone.
